analysis.one_liner: Freezes large agribusiness, food manufacturing, and grocery mergers until antitrust rules are overhauled.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the Senate Judiciary Committee with only 2 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have banned large agribusiness companies, food and beverage makers, and grocery chains from merging with or buying each other until Congress passed broader antitrust legislation for the food sector. It would also have created a 12-member commission to study how much food and farm markets are dominated by a few big firms and recommend changes to the law. Its stated aim was to protect family farmers, food workers, and shoppers from the effects of extreme market concentration.
analysis.who_benefits: Family farmers and ranchers selling into markets where a handful of buyers dominate, food and farm workers whose wages mergers can suppress, rural communities, and grocery shoppers paying a growing gap between farm and retail prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Family farmers, food workers, rural communities, shoppers

how_it_helps.text: Bans mergers and acquisitions among large food and agribusiness firms — those with over $160 million in sales or assets buying firms over $16 million — until Congress enacts comprehensive legislation addressing food-sector concentration; the Attorney General can waive the ban only in extraordinary circumstances such as a firm's insolvency [S3].

Creates a 12-member Food and Agriculture Concentration and Market Power Review Commission, required to include working farmers and ranchers and a representative of organized labor, to study concentration across seeds, processing, meatpacking, retail, and inputs and report recommendations to Congress and the President within about a year [S3].

The bill's findings document the problem it targets: the top four beef packers went from 32% to 85% market share, four firms control about two-thirds of world commodity crop seed, and farmers' share of every retail food dollar fell from 41% in 1950 to under 15% [S3].
It directs the commission to examine whether mergers cause wage suppression, layoffs, and reduced benefits for food-sector workers, and why low farm prices have not lowered supermarket prices [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large agribusiness, meatpackers, seed and chemical companies, and big grocery chains, which could not execute large mergers or acquisitions while the moratorium ran; some transactions that would have produced efficiencies or rescued distressed firms would also have been blocked.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large agribusiness and food retail chains

drawbacks.text: A blanket moratorium is a blunt instrument: it blocks every qualifying deal in the sector, not just harmful ones, and its only waiver is for 'extraordinary circumstances' such as insolvency, so a merger that genuinely improved competition or rescued a distressed supplier could still be prohibited [S3].

The moratorium would last until Congress passes 'comprehensive legislation' addressing food-sector concentration — an open-ended trigger, since Congress could simply never pass such a bill, leaving a standing ban on large food mergers indefinitely [S3].
The bill also authorizes $2 million for the study commission, a modest taxpayer cost [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill directly attacked a documented problem — extreme buyer power over farmers, wage pressure on food workers, and a widening farm-to-shelf price gap — and the main honest objection is that a blanket merger freeze is indiscriminate, hitting harmless or beneficial deals along with harmful ones. The moratorium's open-ended trigger also risked becoming permanent without the study ever producing new law. On balance, the potential gains for farmers, workers, and shoppers were large, but the design traded precision for force.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died there when the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the bill on May 22, 2019, with Sen. Jon Tester as co-introducer [S1][S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day; that was the last action of any kind [S5].
It drew only 2 cosponsors, and the Judiciary Committee never held a markup or sent it to the floor [S4][S5].
The bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, without a hearing, a vote, or a committee report [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meatpackers, seed and agrichemical companies, and big grocery and food-processing firms are better off, because no merger moratorium or concentration review was ever put in place. Farmers, food workers, and shoppers gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate and laid out extensive findings on meatpacking, seed, and grain market concentration.

for.name: 2 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as the bill's only cosponsors.

against.name: Sen. Lindsey Graham
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee of referral, never scheduled a hearing or markup, so the bill never advanced past its first day.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for debate or a vote.

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats sponsored the bill and no votes were ever taken, so no record shows how the chamber would have split; all three named supporters were Democrats.

industries.note: The bill cites the top four beef packers' rise to 85% market share and would have frozen mergers among large processors, ending the deal pipeline that built that share. Its commission would study packer ownership and integration practices that squeeze farmers.

Three firms control about two-thirds of world commodity seed and ~70% of agricultural chemicals, and seed costs for corn farmers nearly quadrupled over 20 years; the moratorium would block further large combinations among these input suppliers.

industries.industry: Grocery retail and food and beverage manufacturing
industries.note: Large grocery chains and food manufacturers with over $160 million in sales would have been barred from acquiring significant rivals until broader antitrust legislation passed. Shoppers pay a growing gap between farm prices and shelf prices.

With fewer and fewer buyers for their crops and livestock, farmers receive a shrinking share of retail food dollars; a merger freeze plus a concentration study directly aimed at raising their bargaining power.
